20421-proserpina-volume-1-studies-of-way:
Proserpina is John Ruskin's study of wayside flowers, written for readers who want to look at plants with care. This first volume grew from Ruskin's own early study of botany. He recalls the first botany book he used, Curtis's Magazine, published in 1795.

Ruskin praises that old magazine's plates as excellent and says he is always glad to find them. His own pages mix close looking at leaves and petals with thoughts on art and naming. The book teaches botany as an act of attention: see the flower rightly, and knowledge follows.
21819-kalli-the-esquimaux-christian-a-me:
Kallihirua, called Kalli, was an Inuk from the far Arctic whose short life is told in this sixpenny memoir by the Reverend T. B. Murray. The book was issued by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge. Kalli was plain and short, the text admits, and looked what he was. Yet all who knew his story and his docile mind felt interest and regard for him.

Brought from his Greenland home into contact with British sailors and teachers, Kalli learned English ways and the Christian faith. Murray, who also wrote on Pitcairn Island, tells the tale for church readers at home. It is a small book with a wide reach: the Arctic, the navy, and the mission field meet in one young life.
21919-teachers-outlines-for-studies-in-e:
High school English teachers get a full set of lesson plans in Gilbert Sykes Blakely's Teachers' Outlines for Studies in English, published in 1908. Blakely taught English at Morris High School in New York City. His outlines follow the college admission requirements of the day, book by book. The novel comes first: he notes that nearly every reading boy and girl loves novels, which gives the teacher a fine opening.

Outlines cover Ivanhoe, Silas Marner, and Cranford, and poems like The Ancient Mariner. Five plays of Shakespeare, plus Comus, and essays from Franklin to Macaulay follow. Each outline points the teaching at the text's heart. The book is a window on the classic school canon of 1908, and on how it was taught.
23167-the-man-in-the-reservoir:
Charles Fenno Hoffman climbs down into trouble in The Man in the Reservoir. Weeds grow from a half-dozen cracks in the masonry, the narrator points out. In one such crack he set his foot and started down the wall. The reservoir then stood fuller than today, its water only a few strides below him.

New York's Croton Reservoir, a city wonder of Hoffman's day, becomes the stage for a rescue remembered in exact, toehold detail. Hoffman, poet and editor, writes the descent as if his reader's foot were on the stone. The tale belongs to the early American magazine tradition, fact and thrill in equal parts. Its masonry still holds.
absalom-s-hair:
Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson's Absalom's Hair opens on Harald Kaas at sixty, a giant gone to seed. His yacht no longer sails the coast in summer, and his club in Christiania sees him rarely. His herculean back is rounded, his teeth blackened by tobacco, and one little finger was bitten off by a man he had knocked down. He caresses the stump while his exploits grow.

Kaas lives at Hellebergene, a coastal estate his father, really a Kurt, reassembled by questionable means. His son Raf must inherit both the estate and its curse of violence. Bjørnson, Norway's national writer, tells a story of inherited temperament: strength curdling across generations. The title recalls the biblical Absalom, undone by pride. Raf's love and his father's shadow drive the short novel. It is among Bjørnson's darkest works, a saga compressed into a modern family tragedy.
ars-recte-vivendi-being-essays-contribut:
George William Curtis gathered Ars Recte Vivendi — the art of living rightly — from his 'Easy Chair' essays in Harper's Magazine. A preface explains that a college professor thought about a dozen of the essays covered the vital questions of hygiene, courtesy. morality well enough to make a book, and Curtis obliged with the collection.

The essays take up extravagance at college, brains and brawn, hazing, and secret societies, then theatre manners, woman's dress, tobacco in health and manners, duelling, and newspaper ethics. Each is short, urbane, and quietly argumentative, in the voice of a man of letters advising the republic on its everyday conduct. Together they form a Gilded Age manual of manners with a moral spine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arthur-marie-: This 1913 reference piece on Arthur-Marie Le Hir — the Sulpician biblical scholar. John Francis Fenlon honors his Hebrew lore. His lectures formed the Paris clergy. The seminary prized his learning. A teacher of the sacred page. His grammar served the Hebrew students.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benadir: This 1913 reference piece on Benadir — the Somali coast's missions. Albert Battandier tells its hard story. The priests braved the desert shore. The missions' foothold was dearly won. The Church's Indian Ocean frontier. Its dhow harbor faces the ocean. Its missions face the desert winds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-o-bruad: A 1913 entry on David O'Bruadair — the Irish bard. John MacErlean honors his famous verse. His pen sang the Gaelic sorrows. The Munster lords prized their poet. The last of the professional bards. His Dáil is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-despair: This 1913 reference piece on despair — the sin against the hopeful virtue. Joseph Delany unfolds its dread nature. The soul despairs of the divine mercy. Judas is the warning's type. The vice of the hopeless heart. Its Cain is the warning type.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hans-burckmai: This 1913 reference piece on Burgkmair — the Augsburg painter. Gerhard Gietmann honors his famous woodcuts. His blocks crowned the imperial books. The age prized the gifted hand. The Dürer's Swabian rival. His 1531 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kafiristan-an: A 1913 entry on Kafiristan and Kashmir — the Himalayan missions. Joseph Cunningham unfolds their rugged tale. The missionaries braved the mountain snows. The missions' foothold was dearly won. The valleys knew their zeal. Their 19th-century missions are famed. Their mountain chapels are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ophir: Ophir was the mysterious land of gold that sent Solomon's ships home laden with treasure. This entry examines the biblical references, the theories of its site, and the legends. The gold country of the Bible: its location has puzzled scholars for ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-iv-the: Philip the Fair was the iron king who crushed the Templars and humbled Boniface VIII. This entry traces his reign, his ministers, and his ruthlessness. The king who cowed the papacy: his ruthless lawyers invented the modern centralized French state.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rusaddir: Rusaddir, the Moroccan port of the North African coast, once had a Christian bishop. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from Mauretania: its dark rocks guard the strait of Gibraltar's mouth in Africa.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sandomir: Sandomir became the diocese of Poland's Vistula towns. This entry covers its bishops, its cathedral, and its history. The faith of the Sandomierz land: its old cathedral crowns the town in Poland's southeast in the Vistula's valley in the hills.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sistine-choir: The Sistine Choir is the pope's own chapel. This entry traces its singers, its polyphony, and its fame. The voices of the Cappella Sistina: their great polyphony crowned the popes in the 1500s' chapel in the Vatican in the Sistina.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-casimir: St. Casimir was the prince of Poland. This entry traces his Cracow, his chastity, and his cult. The lily of the Jagiellon house: his holy tomb crowned Vilna in the 1480s' Lithuania in the chapel of the cathedral in the city.
charles-lamb-a-memoir:
Charles Lamb: A Memoir, by Barry Cornwall, records the essayist Lamb from the memory of one of his last surviving friends. Cornwall was the pen name of Bryan Waller Procter, who writes in May 1866, in his seventy seventh year. He believes himself nearly the only man left who knew Elia intimately. He knew him best in Lamb's final seventeen years or so. He is proud to attach his name to his friend's.

The memoir proceeds by recollection rather than record. A biography of Lamb holds few events. One devotion predominates: the care of his sister Mary, whose madness shadowed both their lives. Anecdotes of the India House clerk who wrote the Essays of Elia, his talk, his jokes, and his tenderness fill the pages. A new generation, Cornwall hopes, will extend its sympathy to a humorist he counts among England's rarest and most delicate.
child-christopher-and-goldilind-the-fair:
William Morris wrote Child Christopher and Goldilind the Fair, published in 1895, one of his late prose romances set in an imagined medieval world. Christopher is the young son of the King of Oakenrealm, stolen as a child and raised as a thrall in a forest house, with no knowledge of his birth. Goldilind is a king's daughter kept a near prisoner by a countess who envies her beauty.

Their paths cross, and the tale follows flight, disguise, battles, and a long road back to rightful rule. Morris tells it in rich, archaic prose thick with woodland, hall, and sea. The romances he wrote in his last years helped found the modern fantasy tale, and this one shows his craft at its ripest.
doe-osti-17076581-insertion-readiness-fo: A reactor steel's radiation trial got its readiness check, and this DOE report covers the A709 irradiation campaign and creep capsule design. The pages detail the prep. The materials team gets its green light. The readiness was insertion. The light was green.
doe-osti-3015786-advancing-a-low-tempera: DAC got low-temp-low-costed, and this DOE text advances organic chemistry capture. The pages detail the findings. The climate folks get their method. The system was direct air capture. The method was climate. The chemistry was organic. The cost was low.
doe-osti-3028687-mechanical-property-mea: HFIR alloys got property-measured, and this DOE text irradiates FM and ODS. The pages detail the mechanical findings. The materials folks get their data. The alloys were irradiated. The data were material. The ODS were FM. The irradiated were alloys.
doe-osti-3366753-reimagining-heating-ven: Manufactured homes got HVAC-reimagined, and this DOE text covers heating ventilation. The pages detail the conditioning findings. The building folks get their data. The conditioning was air. The data were building. The homes were manufactured. The ventilation were heating.
doe-osti-3374045-hsr-lattice-model-in-th: HSR got lattice-modeled, and this DOE text covers hadron beam direction. The pages detail the high findings. The physicists get their data. The harmonics were dipole field. The data were physicist. The HSR were harmonics. The dipole were harmonics.
doe-osti-3488006-analyses-of-cumulus-mix: Cumulus got LES-analyzed, and this DOE text covers aircraft observation mixing. The pages detail the analyses findings. The climate folks get their data. The simulations were LES. The data were climate. The aircraft were ASR. The mixing were cumulus.
doe-osti-3682459-initial-testing-of-the-: FTIR got portable-tested, and this DOE text covers D&P 102 long-wave spectrometers. The pages detail the initial findings. The engineers get their data. The testing was initial. The data were engineer. The 102 were D&P. The long-wave were portable.
doe-osti-3683895-resstock-measure-docume: ResStock got air-sealing-documented, and this DOE documentation covers light attic duct measures. The pages detail the measure findings. The energy folks get their data. The documentation was measure. The data were energy. The attic were insulation. The duct were sealing.
doe-osti-3874839-final-report-on-aluminu: Aluminum 4047 got vendor-reviewed, and this DOE final covers filler wire manufacturers. The pages detail the final findings. The engineers get their closeout. The report was final. The closeout was engineer. The 4047 were filler wire. The vendor were review. The manufacturers were closeout.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIABirdAir_CIA_:
Bird Air was a small airline in Southeast Asia with a long shadow: it grew out of Bird and Sons, a company that flew for the CIA in Laos. Ralph Blumenthal's article, The Mysterious Airlift, follows that airline's strange career.

Proprietary airlines let the agency move men and cargo under commercial cover, and Bird Air's operations sat inside that system during the secret war years. Blumenthal, a New York Times reporter, traces the company through its contracts and questions. The article preserves investigative reporting on the CIA's air arm, where the paperwork was meant to say as little as possible.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAGeorgeClair_:
Clair George ran the CIA's clandestine service as deputy director for operations, and his secret life ended in a courtroom: he was convicted in the Iran-Contra affair. Benjamin Weiser's Washington Post Magazine cover story of May 17, 1992, profiles him at that fall.

Weiser traces George's career through the agency's covert wars to the arms-for-hostages scandal that put his generation of spymasters on trial. The piece is a cover-story portrait: the charming operations chief as a man of the old CIA, overtaken by its exposure. It is preserved complete for readers of intelligence history.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-OswaldAffairLeo:
Gaeton Fonzi reviewed Leo Sauvage's 'The Oswald Affair' for Book Week on October 23, 1966. The review ran under the title 'Burning Questions.' Sauvage, a French journalist, had written one of the first books to dispute the Warren Report. Fonzi examines the contradictions and omissions he found in the official account.

Fonzi later became an investigator for Congress on the same case, which gives his early review a second life. Here, in 1966, he is a reviewer measuring a Frenchman's doubts against the American record. The review marks the moment the Warren Report's critics moved from pamphlets into the book pages of national newspapers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_CH:
Charles Horman and Frank Teruggi were Americans living in Chile when the 1973 coup struck. Both were killed by the military regime. Chile in Their Hearts presents a briefing book built around a new book on their murders.

Their cases became famous through the film Missing and through their families' long search for the truth. The briefing book returns to the documents: what American officials knew, and when they knew it. For readers, the collection joins the personal story of two young men to the paper record of a government that failed to protect them.
l-assommoir:
Émile Zola's novel L'Assommoir is read here in English, in thirteen chapters. It opens with Gervaise, who has waited up until two in the morning for Lantier. She throws herself across the bed, feverish and in tears.

Gervaise, Lantier, and their children eat at a cheap place called the Two-Headed Calf. Lantier stays out late night after night, offering thin excuses. Zola builds the story from such plain, hard details of working life. The novel shows poverty and drink pressing on a Paris family. The title names a cheap drinking shop central to the tale. Work, hunger, and drink grind the family down step by step.
lost-in-the-air:
Lost in the Air is a boys' adventure novel by Roy J. Snell, issued in 1920. It belongs to his Mystery Stories for Boys. The heroes, Bruce Manning and Barney Menter, are young fliers fresh from army air service. They now work in the wilds of northern Canada, near Hudson Bay.

Their flight north brings a strange landing, a walrus hunt, and a battle under the Arctic moon. Chapters promise a treasure city, a mystery cavern, and a wreck. The boys fight criminals and brave the ice to reach the Pole itself. Snell fills the tale with planes, snow, and quick action. It is fast, old-fashioned adventure for young readers.
lothair:
Lothair is a novel by Benjamin Disraeli, the Earl of Beaconsfield. Its hero, Lothair, is a young and wealthy English nobleman. Great forces compete for his soul as he enters the world. The Roman Catholic Church courts him through a charming cardinal and priests.

Secret revolutionary societies also claim him, through the brave Theodora. English country-house society offers him a third, safer path. Disraeli, himself a prime minister, knew this world of power and faith well. The novel mixes romance with sharp talk on religion and politics. It was one of the most debated English novels of its day.
nasa-tm-19700007983-evaluation-with-a-tu:
Willis M. Braithwaite, John H. Dicus, and John E. Moss Jr. ran this study at the Lewis Research Center. Their report came out in January 1970. They used a turbofan engine to test air jets as a way to distort the air flow at the engine inlet.

Engineers need uneven inlet flow to test how an engine behaves in real flight. The team compared air jets with the screens then in common use. Both ways had to make the same half-circle pattern of distorted flow. The results are given as engine stall limits and inlet flow profiles, and the two systems made much the same profiles.
nasa-tm-19700028160-titanium-8al-1mo-1v-:
Ronald L. Nichols of the Manufacturing Engineering Laboratory wrote this report on September 12, 1969. It comes from the Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama. It covers the repair of a crossbeam made of titanium alloy 8Al-1Mo-1V, a structural part whose cracks had to be understood before they could be fixed.

The report opens with the part's history, then moves through testing and a close crack analysis. Photographs show weld seams carrying tungsten left by the electrode, pores with trailing tails, and brittle fracture surfaces under the microscope. The repair section then gives the working steps in order: machining and cleaning first, then welding. Conclusions state what the shop learned from the job.
our-pilots-in-the-air:
Captain William B. Perry's Our Pilots in the Air is a boys' war novel of the First World War's air war in eastern France. Chapter one, A Bombing Air Raid, opens on a Flying Camp in eastern France. Hangars and queer-shaped buildings spread over trampled green. A placard on the bulletin board puts Bombing Squadron members on the alert at seven that evening.

Two young aviators read the notice together: Orry and his smaller, dark-eyed companion. They tease each other about shaking hands on the crank. Their last dive away from a Fokker nearly ended them, until a Tommy in a monoplane helped. Perry writes the new air service as adventure for the boys who were already dreaming of cockpits.
outlaws-of-the-air: George Chetwynd Griffith's Outlaws of the Air is an early novel of aerial warfare. This edition is dated 1897. Griffith pioneered the future-war story in English. The hosted sample shows a contents list only. Its forty-one titles sketch the whole machine. A utopia in the south and the Red Pirate appear. So do the Destroyer at work and the War-Hawk's first flight. No chapter text appears.
poems-of-henry-timrod-with-memoir:
Henry Timrod, the South Carolina poet who became the laureate of the Confederacy, is presented here in a collected Poems with a memoir of his life. An introduction by the late Judge George S. Bryan frames the work. Timrod wrote lyrics of spring, love, and southern landscape before the Civil War consumed his health and his world. He died young, leaving a small body of intensely finished verse.

Contents include Spring, the Cotton Boll, his famous ode on the crop that ruled the South. Courtship poems and serenades, and pieces such as the Arctic Voyager and a Vision of Poesy. Later pages turn to 1866 and the wreckage after defeat. The memoir matters as much as the poems: Timrod's reputation was built posthumously by southern readers who saw their own lost world in his lines. This volume is the shrine they built him.
proserpina-volume-2-studies-of-wayside-f:
John Ruskin continued his studies of wayside flowers in a second volume dated 1888, subtitled with a memory of pure air in the Alps and in his father's Scotland and England. Ruskin planned a new ordering of plants based on close looking.

The volume opens with the violet, whose group he calls the Cytherides, and explains why its placing needs care. Ruskin warns readers not to expect pretty writing, saying that time is past for him. What they get instead is fierce, exact attention to leaf and flower, mixed with grief at a spoiled world.
red-hair:
Elinor Glyn copyrighted this novel in 1905, when it first appeared as The Vicissitudes of Evangeline; the Authors' Press later reissued it as Red Hair. Its heroine writes her own story, starting at Branches Park on November 3. She wonders if it is amusing to be an adventuress, since that is what she expects to become.

She has beauty, skill with hair and hats, and only three hundred pounds a year to live on. Mrs. Carruthers, who raised her, meant to leave her a fortune but made no proper will. The heir takes all, and the girl she detested yet kept is left with nothing but her looks and wit.
samantha-at-the-world-s-fair:
Josiah Allen's Wife, Marietta Holley, wrote Samantha at the World's Fair, illustrated by Baron C. de Grimm and issued at New York in 1893 by Funk and Wagnalls. The book is given to Columbia, who has just sailed out and discovered woman, and to the sect discovered. A front picture shows Samantha and Josiah overwhelmed, the minute they passed the gate, by the unspeakable aspect of the buildings. Copyright was taken in 1893 and the work registered at Stationer's Hall in London.

The preface opens on a beautiful evening in Jonesville, and in the world. The earth sat peaceful and serene under the glowing light of a full moon and some stars. Samantha sat just as peaceful and calm under the mellow light of their hanging lamp. Beside her shone what she calls the blue radiance of her companion's two orbs, meaning Josiah's eyes.
that-mainwaring-affair:
Maynard Barbour wrote That Mainwaring Affair, a mystery novel in twenty-seven chapters. Chapter heads point to a will, an inquest, and a court fight. Titles include The Last Will and Testament of Hugh Mainwaring. The Weaving of the Web and The Silent Witness also stand out.

Chapter one opens on a hot July day. The scene is the plush private offices of Mainwaring and Co., stock brokers. Sun forces thin shafts of light through tight shutters. The light gilds the dim, rich rooms. From that firm base the tale spins out a death. A lost or forged will comes next. Kin then war over a vast estate. Readers get a brisk period mystery of greed, hidden pasts, and proof found at the last hour.
the-bobbsey-twins-at-the-county-fair: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Bobbsey Twins at the County Fair, put out in New York by Grosset and Dunlap with rights dated 1922. A note on the title page says the book was made in war time under state rules to save paper, yet is whole and not cut down. Its first parts are The Broken Bridge, a cry of There's a Snake, The Merry-Go-Round, and A Missing Coat. Sam Is Worried and Happy Days Coming close the part names shown. A plate shows Freddie in a race.
the-book-of-noodles-stories-of-simpleton:
W. A. Clouston wrote The Book of Noodles: Stories of Simpletons; or, Fools and Their Follies, put out in London by Elliot Stock in 1888. Clouston had also written on how folk tales move and change from land to land. He gave the book to his friend David Ross of Glasgow. A line from Twelfth Night stands at the front: this is the best fooling when all is done.

In his preface Clouston says tales of fools, like folk tales at large, have no clear first source. Greek jests of this kind, he thinks, had drifted among many peoples long before they were set in type. The first such tales that can be dated come from old Buddhist books, most of all the Jatakas, or Birth-stories. Those tales were said to have been told by Gautama to his flock, and many deal with silly folk and dull beasts.
the-dialect-of-the-west-of-england-parti: James Jennings, secretary of the Metropolitan Literary Institution, compiled The Dialect of the West of England, particularly Somersetshire. It holds a glossary of words in use there, and pieces showing the dialect. The title page states that the work rests on the second edition. The whole was revised, corrected, and enlarged by James Knight Jennings, M.A., a scholar and librarian. Two dissertations on the Anglo-Saxon pronouns are added. A verse in dialect, from a piece called The Farewell, stands first. Only the front matter is present here.
the-elixir:
Georg Ebers's tale The Elixir opens in Leipzig, in a tall gabled house on Katherinenstrasse long held by his kin. The house, once called The Three Kings, bore the sign of the court apothecary, its three patron saints bright with paint and gold. Ebers says much worth saving happened there, and he means to chronicle his forebear's strange life as his grandmother told it.

That forebear sought a drug to stretch life, and the hunt bent his days. Ebers, an Egyptologist turned novelist, sets the tale in old Leipzig with love for its streets and craft lore.
the-faery-tales-of-weir:
Anna McClure Sholl wrote The Faery Tales of Weir, printed in 1908. Six tales make up the book. They tell of a blue glove and of a golden archer. Other tales bring an invisible wall, a tree in a dark wood, a cat that winked, and magic tears.

The opening paints Weir as a hushed town where real faery tales are still told in shadowy nurseries. Shops have dim, stained windows, houses sleep under thick trees, and small churches ring with hoarse, sweet bells. Into that drowsy, charmed town the tales bring magic objects, hidden walls, and gifts that test the hearts of those who find them.
the-felon-s-track-or-history-of-the-atte:
Michael Doheny wrote The Felon's Track, a history of the failed rising in Ireland that covers the years 1843 to the close of 1848. This Dublin printing of 1920 adds D'Arcy M'Gee's own tale of 1848.

Doheny took part in the Young Ireland movement and fled when the rising fell apart. His book traces the path from open agitation to armed revolt and defeat. A preface, notes on the author's fellows, and an index round out the volume. The title's felon is the hunted rebel, and the track is the road to exile that many such men walked.
the-hosts-of-the-air: Joseph A. Altsheler wrote The Hosts of the Air, subtitled the story of a quest in the Great War, with pictures by Charles Wrenn, published in New York and London by D. Appleton and Company in 1915. Altsheler is named as the author of The Guns of Europe and The Forest of Swords. The pages present add lists for his Civil War series and World War series, naming The Star of Gettysburg and The Guns of Bull Run. Only the title pages and series lists are present here.
the-mastery-of-the-air:
William J. Claxton's The Mastery of the Air deals mainly with real achievements by the pioneers of flight. Claxton states in his preface that the book makes no pretence of going minutely into technical science. His chief object is to wake an intelligent interest in flying among ordinary readers. The Great War, he notes, gave a tremendous impetus to the contest for mastery of the air.

The opening part treats balloons and airships, starting with man's duel with nature. A chapter credits a French paper-maker with inventing the balloon. Claxton thanks the Royal Flying Corps and the Royal Naval Air Service for illustrations and information. Aviation firms such as Sopwith and A. V. Roe also helped him. Readers get the romance of early flight and wartime flying, written for the general public rather than the expert.
the-oakdale-affair:
Edgar Rice Burroughs wrote The Oakdale Affair, a tale that opens at night outside a banker's house. A young prowler watches the house of Jonas Prim, president of the First National Bank of Oakdale, and notes that the family is at dinner and the upper floor is empty. The youth has already stolen a suit and cap from the chauffeur's rooms above the garage.

Burroughs stresses that the intruder is no hardened thief. The boy's strained face and slender build suggest a beginner steeling himself for a crime. He crosses the lawn boldly, passes the open hall door on purpose, and seems to know the house and its habits well.
the-open-air: Richard Jefferies gathered his nature papers under the title The Open Air. In a short note he thanks the editors of The Standard, Longman's Magazine, the Manchester Guardian, and other papers where the pieces first appeared. That note and a contents list are the whole of what is present; the essays themselves are absent. The contents list Saint Guido, Wild Flowers, Sunny Brighton, The Pine Wood, Nature on the Roof, The Modern Thames, The Haunt of the Hare, Downs, and Forest.
the-philosophy-of-despair:
David Starr Jordan wrote The Philosophy of Despair, dedicated to John Maxson Stillman in token of good cheer. A poem at the front imagines his epitaph on a stone by the sea: jungle and town and reef and sea, I loved God's earth and his earth loved me. The essay then declares that today is the only day we have, the day in which we play our part.

Our part, Jordan says, is action, not whining, and love, not cynicism, expressed as human helpfulness. Any other course leads toward decay and waste. He takes his text from FitzGerald's version of the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, quoting the angel of the darker drink. Despair, in his handling, becomes a call to work.
the-poetical-works-of-henry-kirk-white-w: The Poetical Works of Henry Kirke White comes with a memoir by Sir Harris Nicolas. Here only the title page, dedication, and contents appear, so the poems themselves are absent. After the memoir, miscellaneous poems are listed: Clifton Grove, Time, and Childhood in two parts. The Christiad appears too. Other entries include lines on a survey of the heavens, a summer's eve description, and verses in the prospect of death. Nelsoni Mors appears, plus an elegy for Mr. Gill, drowned in the Trent while bathing.
the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendell-hol:
The Iron Gate and Other Poems (1877 to 1881) form this section of Holmes's Poetical Works, bracketed as Volume 3 of the 1893 set. The contents list verses for Whittier's seventieth birthday and the Moore centennial. The American Academy centennial appears, and the Massachusetts Medical Society's centennial dinner. The School-Boy and The Silent Melody appear too.

The opening poem, The Iron Gate, was read at the breakfast given in honour of Holmes's seventieth birthday by the publishers of the Atlantic Monthly at Boston on December 3, 1879. It begins by asking where this patriarch is whom the company is kindly greeting. The name is not unfamiliar, the poem says. Nor is it unknown to many a joyous meeting in days long vanished. The question hanging over the verse is whether he is still the same, or changed by years, forgotten and forgetting.
the-poetical-works-of-william-lisle-bowl: Volume I of The Poetical Works of William Lisle Bowles was edited by the Reverend George Gilfillan, with memoir and explanatory notes. James Nichol published it at Edinburgh in 1855. Bowles is styled canon of St. Paul's Cathedral and rector of Bremhill. Here only the title pages and the start of the contents appear, so the poems themselves are absent. The contents open with sonnets at Tynemouth Priory after a tempestuous voyage and at Bamborough Castle. Others stand on the Wainsbeck, Tweed, and Itchin, and one marks resigning an Oxford scholarship.
the-war-in-the-air:
H. G. Wells wrote The War in the Air in 1907, and a preface to the reprint edition, signed K., asks readers to grasp that date firmly. The novel appeared as a serial in 1908 and in book form that fall. Aeroplanes were then a rumour for most people, and the sausage balloon held the air.

The preface concedes weak spots: few anti-aircraft guns and still less thought of submarines. Yet Prince Karl, a fantasy in 1908, has since been copied faithfully by reality, the preface claims. Wells's warning stands: continued war means civilisation's smash-up, leaving a choice between chaos and a united world. Contents chapters send Bert Smallways from a balloon into a German air-fleet, a battle over the North Atlantic, and war coming to New York.
